Executive Summary
Each year the American Society of Naval Engineers (ASNE) hosts a national Promoting Electric
Propulsion (PEP) competition. During this competition, university teams design both manned
and unmanned boats for a 2-mile time trial in April.
As this will be Elon’s second year competing, we are able to rely on the previous team’s design
and documentation, help from Elon educators such as Matthew Banks, Will Pluer, and Jonathan
Su as well as Matthew Briscoe as the ASNE educator in residence.
Through the process of redesigning the vessel we mainly focused on improving the hull’s
efficiency and increasing power to the motor while making the necessary adjustments for the
rudder and propellors to handle the increased forces the increased forces. This report will break
down the design process of developing these improvements while maintaining adherence to the
competition’s guidelines.

Design Overview
Research and Background
Early in our research we divided the boat into five unique subsystems and assigned them to the
team members to which they were best suited. This allowed the team to utilize our preexisting
knowledge efficiently to narrow down the exact areas that each subsystem needed to be
improved on. Fortunately, the previous team kept documentation for all their major decisions
which allowed us a good starting point for our research. Looking through that documentation, we
decided to keep the propellor and controller choice while upscaling every other aspect of the
boat.
While the previous team’s goal was to simply finish the race, our goal includes an expected
finish time of 10 minutes. To accomplish this, we needed to improve many parts of the boat. The
two biggest items on the list were the hull and the motor. The previous hull design was a flatbottom displacement hull, which prioritized stability over speed. We changed this to a semi-deep
V design, allowing the boat to cut through water and waves easier. This design also decreases the
hydrodynamic drag of the vessel, which becomes increasingly important as the speed of the boat
increases.

Propulsion (PEP) competition. During this competition, university teams design both manned
and unmanned boats for a 2-mile time trial in April.
As this will be Elon’s second year competing, we are able to rely on the previous team’s design
and documentation, help from Elon educators such as Matthew Banks, Will Pluer, and Jonathan
Su as well as Matthew Briscoe as the ASNE educator in residence.
Through the process of redesigning the vessel we mainly focused on improving the hull’s
efficiency and increasing power to the motor while making the necessary adjustments for the

down the design process of developing these improvements while maintaining adherence to the
competition’s guidelines.




Design Overview
Research and Background
Early in our research we divided the boat into five unique subsystems and assigned them to the
team members to which they were best suited. This allowed the team to utilize our preexisting
knowledge efficiently to narrow down the exact areas that each subsystem needed to be
improved on. Fortunately, the previous team kept documentation for all their major decisions
which allowed us a good starting point for our research. Looking through that documentation, we
decided to keep the propellor and controller choice while upscaling every other aspect of the
boat.

While the previous team’s goal was to simply finish the race, our goal includes an expected
finish time of 10 minutes. To accomplish this, we needed to improve many parts of the boat. The
two biggest items on the list were the hull and the motor. The previous hull design was a flat-
bottom displacement hull, which prioritized stability over speed. We changed this to a semi-deep
V design, allowing the boat to cut through water and waves easier. This design also decreases the
hydrodynamic drag of the vessel, which becomes increasingly important as the speed of the boat
increases.

pages.text:
Figures 1 & 2: CAD models of the previous and current designs.

We increased the motor’s power supply by replacing the previous four 12V, 10Ah LiFePO4
batteries with eight 12V, 100Ah LiFePO4 batteries. This totals to a 52V, 200Ah circuit, a 900%
increase in power from last year. To help make the most of this increase in power, we upgraded
the previous 3kW e-foil motor to a 9kW version. With these two changes, we can expect the boat
to reach the 12-mph minimum required speed to complete the course in 10 minutes.
The steering system needs to be able to withstand higher speeds and saltwater corrosion while
still being lightweight and machinable. To ensure this durability, 5052 and 6061 aluminum was
chosen for their increased strength and welding capability. Stress calculations were then
performed to ensure proper dimensioning and validate safety requirements. The servo used to
rotate the shaft is an RC servo with a 550kg-cm max torque, giving us a torsional safety factor of
2.93 with the existing rudder geometry.
Overall, we were able to identify key areas of improvement for the boat to reach the target as
well as direct ways to enhance those systems. We also built up the other subsystems to account
for the increased forces associated with the higher speeds the boat is expected to reach.

Design
Following our research, we delved into the more specific points of the design process. This
process required constant communication between subsystems as each minute change had
ramifications for the entire system. With the change to a V-hull we had to create a section for the
placement of the motor mount. To do this, we created a small step to a flat section near the back
of the boat to allow for the placement of the motor mount. This step was then further utilized as
the starting height for the internal floor of the boat. With the floor now at a set level, we designed
specific cutouts beneath it for the ballast that needs to be added for both our testing and
competition. Finally, with the increase in total battery size, we had to increase the length of the
hull to over nine feet.

pages.text:
Figure 3: Complete CAD assembly of the boat hull, with battery volumes included.

After initial testing of the boat hull, the next task was to integrate the batteries into the system in
a safe and controlled manner. Unlike the previous year, the batteries take up too much space to
be put in a box. Our plan instead was to have a good margin from the waterline to the lip of the
hull to minimize water intake. Our early tests vindicate this as safe enough connection and when
we modeled the batteries’ heat through a SOLIDWORKS thermal simulation, we did not see
evidence that the batteries would overheat to the point of breaking down or experiencing a
noticeable decrease in power. However, if this does not prove sufficient for water safety as we
progress through our testing, our other option is a light foam top to seal onto the hull, creating a
watertight seal. This would increase the risk of the batteries overheating but should completely
prevent water from contacting the batteries. For both situations the batteries would be secured
onto the wooden floor of the boat using high strength Velcro.

Figure 4: Initial electrical testing of the batteries in circuit.

As previously mentioned, we sized up the motor from 3kWs to 9kWs. With this change comes an
increase in weight and therefore a change to the motor mount. Our new design provides more
reinforcement for the connection to the boat while allowing for a faster setup. The mount is made
of 6061 aluminum to provide the strength to deal with the extra motor weight while not adding
excess weight itself. It only requires six total bolts (four M4 and two 1/4-20), for total assembly
through utilizing the mounting features present on the motor itself. The geometry of the aligns
itself with the primary plate, allowing the nuts to be tightened easily. With this design the motor
is stable and the assembly time of the mount is decreased to below 1 minute.

pages.text:
Figure 5: Functional mockup with Flipsky motor attached to the mounting fixture using 3D-printed motor mounts.

The final rudder design is an outboard rudder completely independent of the propulsion
subsystem. It operates with a push/pull connection to the servo and is designed with the least
number of linkages possible, minimizing potential failure points. The design was also made to be
easy to redesign, repair, and replace, making it the optimal option for testing.
Because this design uses a 550kg-cm RC servo, two LifePO4 12V 25Ah batteries are needed to
power it. These batteries were put in series and connected directly to the servo. The servo is then
connected directly to the Flysky receiver, which is connected to the VESC for the motor
controller. This wiring allows convenient testing of the servo without the VESC.

System Breakdown
We made major changes to most subsystems of the boat. We changed the hull from a flat-bottom
displacement hull to a semi-deep v design, allowing for more maneuverability in the water while
decreasing the drag coefficient. This, combined with increased power from our new power
supply of 52.4V, 100 Ah per battery string should result in a dramatic increase in top speed. We
also have two LiFePO4 12V 25Ah batteries to power the rudder servo which is then directly
connected to the receiver.

We are carrying over the control system from the previous year as it was intuitive and had no
noticeable downsides. The difference being that we do not have a pump and therefore have no
need for a pump actuation switch. Channel 2 will continue to control the power of the motor, and
channel 4 will continue to control the position of the rudder.

Testing and Performance
During our initial testing for the boat, we discovered that our buoyancy calculations were too
conservative. The boat was over-buoyant. This meant it lacked stability when in the water,
something that we knew from the previous year’s competition is vital to completing the course.
Because of this we designed a weighted skeg to both increase the weight of the boat and lower its
center of mass. This addition proved successful and made a large difference to the stability of the
boat.

reinforced parts of the rudder system and touched up the welding done on the skeg and motor
mounts. Fortunately, the major components of the hull and batteries have not experienced any

Testing and Performance
During our initial testing for the boat, we discovered that our buoyancy calculations were too
conservative. The boat was over-buoyant. This meant it lacked stability when in the water,
something that we knew from the previous year’s competition is vital to completing the course.
Because of this we designed a weighted skeg to both increase the weight of the boat and lower its

During testing we also discovered various small errors made during our design processes. We
reinforced parts of the rudder system and touched up the welding done on the skeg and motor
mounts. Fortunately, the major components of the hull and batteries have not experienced any

pages.text:
signs of damage or wear, with the batteries specifically staying in line with the SOLIDWORKS
thermal simulation done previously.

During our initial testing we found that the controller is quite sensitive due to the various
upgrades made to both the power and control systems. With continued practice during testing
and a dedicated pilot, this should not pose an issue to the handling of the boat.

Figure 7: Buoyancy test of the boat with half of the batteries in place

Future Development
There is still a multitude of improvements that could be made to the boat. During the process of
researching motors we were brought into contact with Havoc AI who allowed us access to their
Torqeedo 6.0T motors. These were not a part of this year’s design despite delivering substantially
higher torque than the current e-foil solution because of the associated increase in weight. Future
teams will still have access to this partnership and could work towards utilizing those motors for
another substantial increase in power.
The other main improvement that could be made is the maneuverability of the boat. While it is
more agile than the previous design, with the increased speeds that come from a more powerful
motor and batteries it is still difficult to maneuver. There is still a risk of tipping should the boat
turn too quickly. Creating a more stable weight distribution and a more dynamic rudder system
would allow the boat to take sharper turns with increased stability, further saving time during the
competition.

Conclusion
Our team would like to thank Michael Briscoe and the ASNE for their continuous support
throughout this project. We would also like to thank Havoc AI and Metal Works for providing us
with options for our designs while staying within our budget. They allowed us to push ourselves
and this project as far as we could take it. We have worked hard the past year and are proud of
what we have been able to accomplish.
